source.title: On the Spectral Bias of Deep Neural Networks
source.authors: Nasim Rahaman; A. Baratin; Devansh Arpit; Felix Dräxler; Min Lin; F. Hamprecht; Yoshua Bengio; Aaron C. Courville

record.tranche_reason: The paper measures learning order and fitting difficulty in synthetic and MNIST experiments, using spectral components and loss curves rather than random-label classification in the original settings.
record.gate_note: The paper cites Zhang et al. (2017a) and Arpit et al. (2017) for fitting random mappings and for the i.i.d.-noise validation dip; those cited results are not this study's results. Its own Experiment 8 compares fitting white-noise targets on two input manifolds. Experiments 3 and 4 add structured frequency noise to MNIST targets.
record.test_reason: Experiments 3–4 test V6 by tracking learning of real MNIST targets and added structured noise during training. The study is not an original source. Its spectral and validation-loss measurements provide a different method for examining signal-before-noise learning.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors conclude that ReLU networks favor lower-frequency functions, demonstrate this learning bias on synthetic and MNIST regression tasks, and show that complex manifold geometry can facilitate expressing high-frequency targets through lower-frequency network functions.
record.recipe_differences: Studies frequency-component learning and structured-noise regression, with a separate white-noise regression comparison across input manifolds; not the original random-label classification recipe. The Experiment 1 network uses full-batch Adam, and the authors explicitly avoid stochastic gradient descent there.
record.method_sensitivity: Noise frequency and amplitude affect validation behavior; data-manifold shape affects white-noise fitting difficulty.

fits_no_version.finding: Identical networks find white-noise scalar targets harder to fit on MNIST autoencoder reconstructions than on a flat manifold of the same nominal dimension.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Input-manifold geometry affects the difficulty of fitting independent random regression targets.

fits_no_version.finding: Lower-frequency components of synthetic sinusoidal regression targets are learned first, even when higher-frequency components have larger amplitudes.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: ReLU networks exhibit frequency-dependent learning speed on synthetic regression targets.

fits_no_version.finding: Increasing the complexity of flower-shaped input manifolds facilitates fitting higher-frequency targets.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Manifold geometry changes the effective spectral bias of a neural network.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML), Proceedings of the 36th International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 97, 2019
record.problems: The random-target result is a figure-only comparison of training loss on two manifolds, with no stated architecture details in Appendix A.6 and no numeric values in the text. The MNIST noise experiments use structured frequency noise and regression, not random-label classification. Experiment 1 uses full-batch Adam rather than stochastic gradient descent.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-version rows omitted. Synthetic sinusoid learning-order and manifold-shape results are outside the listed versions and are summarized under fits_no_version.

untested.parts: Near-zero training classification error on completely random labels, chance test performance, and unchanged architecture and training hyperparameters relative to true-label training.
Random-versus-true-label training-time factors and convergence as the fraction of corrupted labels increases.
Perfect fitting of shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs.
A random-label corruption-fraction sweep with perfect training fit and steadily deteriorating test classification performance.
Effects of weight decay, dropout, and data augmentation on random-label fitting and true-label generalization.
Learning order with independently randomized classification labels; the study's own MNIST experiments use additive structured noise and regression.

record.verdict_notes: Remove the record's V1 limits_scope verdict: R4 measures a different outcome. The lack of random-label classification experiments belongs under untested, not as a V6 scope limitation. Claims about perfect random-label fitting and the i.i.d.-noise classification validation dip are attributed to prior studies.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test fully random image-label assignments with the original models, stochastic gradient methods, test error at chance, or unchanged hyperparameters.
Does not compare training time for random labels versus true labels or sweep the fraction of corrupted labels.
Does not test shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs.
Does not vary the fraction of randomly corrupted labels from none to all or measure classification test error under that sweep.
Does not test weight decay, dropout, or data augmentation against random-label fitting or true-label generalization.
Tests learning order for MNIST targets with added structured frequency noise and for synthetic frequency components; does not directly test random labels or the original classification setup.

rows.measure: Validation loss on a separate subset evaluated against the unnoised true target; low-frequency noise adversely affected validation performance, and the paper reports that the network readily fits this noise.

rows.note: Text describes the direction of the result but gives no numeric values. The paired β settings are not individually recoverable from the supplied Results text.
rows.check: Low-frequency noise is readily fitted and harms validation performance, qualifying the signal-before-noise pattern. This does not establish reversed learning order. The two amplitude conditions should be separated if their curves can be recovered; their numerical values are unavailable in the supplied text.

rows.subject: two identical networks (architecture not stated in Appendix A.6)
rows.operation_detail: Regressed white-noise scalar targets on MNIST reconstructions from a denoising autoencoder versus 64-dimensional random vectors embedded in the input space.

white noise, scalars sampled from U([0, 1])

rows.measure: Training loss curves; paper states that learning random labels is harder when inputs lie on the MNIST-like manifold than on the flat 64-dimensional manifold.
rows.baseline: The 64-dimensional random-vector flat manifold is the comparison condition.
rows.value: Figure-only loss curves; the MNIST-manifold condition is described as harder to solve.
rows.note: This is a regression comparison using white-noise targets, not a test of random image-label classification, test error at chance, or zero training error. The figure does not provide recoverable numeric values.
rows.check: White-noise scalar regression compared across input manifolds measures relative fitting difficulty. It establishes neither near-zero random-label classification error under V1 nor real-before-noise learning under V6. It also lacks V2's true-label timing comparison.

relationships.display_finding: Clean targets were learned near the early validation-loss minimum before higher-frequency noise, with one transition around iteration 200.
